title: Design an ML Content Moderation System at Scale
prompt: Design a content moderation system for a large user-generated-content platform. It must screen text, images, and video across many policy categories (violence, hate, sexual content, spam, self-harm), combine automated ML with human reviewers, and give users an appeals process. Assume very high upload volume and strict latency needs for the publish path.
blurb: Multimodal T&S at scale: policy classifiers, human-in-the-loop routing, appeals, and keeping models aligned with shifting policy.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (multi-category classification across modalities, block/limit/allow actions, human review, appeals, escalation) from non-functional (publish-path latency, high recall on egregious harms, reviewer throughput, auditability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about content types, sync-block vs async-review policy, legal/regulatory categories (CSAM, terrorism), cost of over- vs under-blocking, appeal SLAs, languages/regions.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives uploads/sec, per-modality inference cost (cheap text vs expensive video), GPU fleet sizing, human-review capacity vs auto-decision rate, storage for content + decisions.

rubric.label: Multimodal classification pipeline
rubric.description: Per-modality models (text, image, video frames, audio), hashing/matching for known-bad content, staged cheap-to-expensive cascade, fusion across signals.

rubric.label: Human-in-the-loop routing
rubric.description: Confidence-band routing to reviewers, prioritized queues by harm severity, reviewer tooling, capturing reviewer decisions as labels, active learning on uncertain cases.

rubric.label: Appeals & feedback
rubric.description: Appeal workflow, re-review, overturn tracking, using appeals/overturns as a quality and label signal, avoiding feedback-loop bias.

rubric.label: Training-serving parity & labels
rubric.description: Consistent preprocessing across train/serve, label provenance (reviewer vs appeal vs golden set), handling policy changes that relabel old data, inter-annotator agreement.

rubric.label: Evaluation & drift
rubric.description: Per-category precision/recall at operating points, golden sets, prevalence estimation, drift from new harmful trends/adversarial evasion, monitoring auto-decision quality.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Ingest → hash-match → modality classifiers (cascade) → decision/policy engine → auto-action or review queue → appeals; async re-scan of published content.

rubric.label: Scaling & reliability
rubric.description: GPU autoscaling, batching, async video processing, backpressure, graceful degradation (default action when models unavailable), regional/language scaling.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Category-level metrics, queue depth/latency, reviewer agreement, model version tracking, prevalence dashboards, alert on spikes of a harm category.

rubric.label: Safety, privacy & abuse
rubric.description: Handling illegal content (secure pipelines, legal reporting), reviewer wellbeing, adversarial evasion, PII/privacy, audit trail for regulators and appeals.

functional_requirements: Classify text, image, and video against multiple policy categories
Match content against hashes of known-bad media (e.g. CSAM/terrorism databases)
Take graduated actions: allow, age-gate/limit reach, remove, escalate
Route uncertain or high-severity content to human reviewers
Provide an appeals workflow and re-review
Feed reviewer/appeal decisions back as training labels
nonfunctional_requirements: Low added latency on the synchronous publish path; heavy analysis async
Very high recall on egregious/illegal harms (miss-cost dominates)
Reviewer throughput and prioritization by severity
Full auditability of automated + human decisions for appeals and regulators
clarifying_questions: Which categories, and which are legally mandated (must-block, must-report)?
Do we block synchronously at publish, or allow-then-scan asynchronously per category?
Relative cost of over-blocking (false removal) vs under-blocking (harm reaches users)?
How many languages/regions and how localized is policy?
Upload volume and content-type mix (text vs image vs video)?
qualifying_questions: Is content mostly short text, or media-heavy (video is far more expensive)?
Real-time feeds/live streams, or only stored uploads?
One global policy or region-specific rules?

estimations.traffic: ~1M uploads/min ≈ ~17K uploads/sec at peak; ~70% text, ~25% image, ~5% video
estimations.inference_cost: Text classify ~2-5ms CPU; image ~20-50ms GPU; video = sample N frames + audio → 10-100x image cost
estimations.gpu_fleet: Media share × QPS × per-inference GPU-ms → thousands of GPU cores; batch to raise utilization
estimations.review_capacity: If 2% of content routes to humans at 17K/s that's ~340/s → infeasible manually; auto-decision the high-confidence mass, route only uncertain/severe
estimations.storage: Content refs + decision logs + feature/embedding cache; retain decisions long-term for appeals/audit; retain flagged media under strict controls

data_model: content(content_id PK, author_id, type, uri, created_at, status)
moderation_decisions(content_id, category, score, action, decided_by, model_version, ts)
review_tasks(task_id, content_id, priority, queue, assignee, resolution, ts)
labels(content_id, category, label, source, annotator_id, agreement)
api_design: POST /v1/moderate { content_id, type, uri|payload } → { decision, category_scores{}, action, model_version }  (sync fast-path; heavy work async)
POST /v1/review/{task_id}/resolve { action, categories[] } → records reviewer label
GET /v1/content/{id}/status → current enforcement state + audit trail
reference.high_level_design: On upload the gateway runs cheap synchronous checks — perceptual/hash matching against known-bad databases and a fast text classifier — to block the clearly-illegal immediately. Media goes to an async cascade: cheap models first, expensive image/video/audio models only on content that survives. A fusion/decision engine combines model scores, hash hits, author reputation, and policy rules to pick an action. High-confidence content is auto-actioned; content in the uncertain confidence band or above a severity threshold is routed to prioritized human-review queues. Reviewer decisions and appeal outcomes flow into a label store that feeds active-learning sampling and periodic retraining. A prevalence/drift monitor tracks per-category quality and emerging harmful trends, and models roll out through golden-set evaluation and shadow testing.

deep_dives.probe: Video moderation is expensive. Design a cheap-to-expensive cascade — hash match, then light model, then heavy model — so you spend GPU only where needed. Where do you set the gates?
You can't send everything to humans. How do you decide what to auto-action vs route to review, and how do you prioritize the queue when a harm spikes?
Reviewers disagree and policy changes over time. How do you manage label quality, inter-annotator agreement, and relabeling old data when policy shifts?

For CSAM/terrorism the miss-cost is catastrophic; for borderline speech, over-removal is the risk. How do per-category operating points and actions differ, and how do you measure recall on rare egregious content?
Appeals overturn some automated removals. How do you feed overturns back without creating a biased feedback loop where the model only ever learns from what it already flagged?
Bad actors mutate images/text to evade classifiers. How do you detect and adapt to evasion, and how does that change your drift monitoring?

Author reputation and account state (prior strikes, verified status) live in a separate service and change constantly. How do those changes propagate into the moderation decision path so you're not scoring on stale author signals?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions feature or reputation or embedding
followup_bank.question: When an author's reputation or account state changes in the source system, how does the moderation pipeline's feature/embedding store stay in sync — change-stream/CDC into the store, or scheduled recompute? What staleness is acceptable?
You're caching embeddings / near-duplicate signatures. What's the eviction policy, and when the underlying policy or content changes, how do you invalidate stale-after-change cache entries?
How do you roll out a new classifier safely — golden-set eval, shadow mode, per-category operating points, and rollback on what signal?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions human or reviewer or queue
followup_bank.question: How do you prioritize the review queue during a harm spike, and how do you capture reviewer decisions as high-quality labels?
How do you prevent appeals/overturn feedback from biasing the model toward only re-learning what it already flags?
Media inference is expensive — describe your cheap-to-expensive cascade and where GPU batching helps.

scaling: GPU autoscaling with request batching for image/video models
Async, queue-backed media processing decoupled from the publish path
Shard hash-match and classifier fleets by modality/region
Backpressure + default-action policy when models are saturated
bottlenecks: Video/audio inference GPU cost and latency
Human-review capacity as the hard ceiling
Hot queues during coordinated harm spikes
Embedding/near-dup index growth for duplicate detection
tradeoffs: Sync block (safe, adds latency) vs allow-then-scan (fast, brief exposure)
High recall on harm vs over-removal / free-expression cost
Bigger multimodal model (better) vs GPU cost + latency
Global model (consistent) vs localized models (culturally accurate)
alternative_solutions: Rules + keyword lists (cheap, brittle, easily evaded)
Single multimodal foundation model vs specialized per-category classifiers
Fully async moderation with reactive user reporting as a safety net
Federated hash-sharing with industry databases for known-bad media
observability: Per-category precision/recall at operating points vs golden sets
Queue depth + review latency by severity
Prevalence dashboards and spike alerts per category
Model version + traffic split; embedding index freshness
security: Secure, access-controlled pipelines for illegal content + legal reporting duties
Adversarial evasion monitoring and rapid model updates
PII minimization and privacy in stored content/decisions
Immutable audit trail of automated + human decisions for regulators and appeals
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer keeps the synchronous publish path cheap (hash-matching known-bad + a fast text model) and pushes expensive multimodal analysis into an async cheap-to-expensive cascade that spends GPU only on content that survives earlier stages. It treats humans as a scarce resource: auto-decide the high-confidence mass, route only the uncertain confidence band and high-severity items to prioritized queues, and turn reviewer and appeal decisions into labels via active learning. It sets per-category operating points reflecting asymmetric cost — very high recall for illegal/egregious harm, caution against over-removal for borderline speech — and evaluates with per-category precision/recall against golden sets plus prevalence estimation, not accuracy. It handles policy change and annotator disagreement in labeling, guards against appeal feedback-loop bias, and monitors drift from adversarial evasion and emerging harmful trends as a first-class concern, with safe golden-set/shadow model rollout and full auditability.
reference.note_on_realism: Keep discussion educational and framework-based; do not produce operational detail about creating harmful content or evading real safety systems.

interviewer_notes: This is a trust-and-safety systems problem, not just a classifier. Push the candidate to separate the fast synchronous publish path from heavy async analysis early, and to justify sync-block vs allow-then-scan per category by harm cost. The senior separators: (1) treating human review as a scarce, prioritized resource with confidence-band routing and active learning, and (2) per-category evaluation with asymmetric cost — reject 'accuracy'/single-threshold thinking and make them reason about recall on rare egregious content and prevalence estimation. When they place a feature/embedding store or author-reputation signal, hit the CDC/freshness probe about how source changes propagate. When they add an embedding or near-duplicate cache, probe eviction and stale-after-change invalidation. Also probe adversarial evasion and appeals feedback-loop bias. Keep the conversation educational and framework-level; do not let it drift into how-to detail about producing or evading detection of harmful content. Reserve time for drift monitoring and safe model rollout via golden sets.
